notes: F3 reader copy edit (2026-10-07): presentation fields only. Branch thesis <=45 words (one or two sentences) and reader_hook <=60 words; node titles <=60 characters with jargon expanded. No numbers, years, bands or claims changed.

patch.thesis: If research-grade AI math reaches outside engineers in 2027 (base case) and checking is cheap, on-demand analysis spreads through space engineering by 2028. New program schedules shrink about a quarter to a third (38% at most), since tests, factories and launches run on physical time.
patch.reader_hook: A research-grade result costs about $200-2,000 in tokens (the low figure counts only published successes), so 1,000 hard problems a year cost one to ten engineers before checking. Checking sets the price. Yet only about a third of a program's critical path is cognitive, so Amdahl's law caps base-case schedule compression at about 38%; realized gains are likelier 20-30%.

patch.thesis: If AI settles famous fluid problems, up to unforced Navier-Stokes, the theorems change almost no engine, heat shield or orbit. Engineers get the proof machinery and on-demand error bars as verification evidence from about 2028 (base case), and math stops being a bottleneck around 2029.
patch.reader_hook: An AI agent formalized a Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau plasma result in 10 days for about $200, with no human-written code (one mathematician, 229 prompts). Two of its three failure modes, hypothesis creep and definition-alignment bugs, came from stating the problem. Only 16 partial-differential-equation and 12 dynamics families sit among the release's 372, because that is what was posed.

patch.thesis: If AI agents can draft specifications and machine-checked proofs for flight code, verified code gets 15-120x cheaper per line by 2028-29 and flies widely from 2029-30 (base case). Regulators accept proof-based plans around 2030 (Medium); engine, entry, launch-safety and crewed credit stay Low by 2031.
patch.reader_hook: A fully verified line of flight code falls from about $300-600 to about $5-20 by 2028-29 (base case), yet a highest-criticality (Level A) program gets only about 2x cheaper (1.8-2.4x). And in all 9 software- or logic-related losses and near-losses among 12 notable cases, from Ariane 501 to Athena, a wrong assumption or spec was the missing piece.

patch.thesis: If AI proves routing and interference bounds, constellation meshes and direct-to-device service run on certified plans by 2029-30 (base case, Medium). Spectrum treaties (nothing before WRC-31), quantum links and encryption upgrades move at regulatory and hardware speed; cheaper AI code-breaking estimates make upgradeable encryption urgent.
patch.reader_hook: The FCC's 2026 rules (FCC 24-117 and FCC 26-26) replace fixed power masks with private coordination judged against simulated performance criteria: 3% throughput loss and 0.1% (geostationary) or 0.4% (non-geostationary) added unavailability. FCC 26-26 also lifted the cap on same-frequency beams per location, turning spectrum rights into a math problem.

patch.thesis: Commercial operators fly new hardware qualified mainly by AI analysis around 2029-30 (base case, Medium); government and crewed programs wait for a rulebook (2029, Medium) and broader credit (2030, Low). Analysis runs 2-5x faster, but test stands keep qualification only 10-20% shorter by 2031.
patch.reader_hook: Much of what 'certification by analysis' promises exists without AI: NASA-STD-5001B lets some metal structures skip strength tests. Skipping a launch vehicle's primary-structure qualification article saves tens of millions of dollars and up to a year. The base case puts the first AI-backed government credit beyond today's allowances around 2030-31, against 2040-2050 in NASA-sponsored studies of aircraft certification by analysis.

patch.thesis: If AI can certify combustion, flow and materials models, engines could earn model-based reuse life from about 2029 and an AI-designed alloy could fly by 2031 (Low in the base case, Medium in S3). Engines stay test-paced: each failure mode costs a redesign and re-test.
patch.reader_hook: Proving 0.99 engine reliability at 90% confidence takes about 230 zero-failure starts. A high-cadence Starship fleet logs that many in a handful of flights, so finding and fixing failure modes paces engines. In an illustrative model, a validated boil-off model saves about 0-1 of the 1-5 extra tanker flights per lunar-lander refueling campaign, at one tanker every 6 days.

patch.thesis: With on-demand AI uncertainty analysis, commercial capsules fly thinner heat shields around 2030 (base case, Medium). Starship-scale shield reuse comes around 2030 from flight data, with AI adding months; routine reentry, heavy Mars landings and point-to-point cargo wait on demand, launch windows and regulation.
patch.reader_hook: For NASA's now-cancelled Mars Sample Retrieval Lander, a Monte Carlo at one stressing point found a heat shield at ~75% of baseline thickness kept its adhesive bondline below the limit in ~99% of cases. But it sampled heating error only up to existing margins, while at that 8 km/s entry the radiation model under-predicted shock-tube data by up to 2x.

patch.thesis: SpaceX's hardware, launch and capital clock paces orbital compute: 100-kW-class satellites fly about 2028 and earn revenue about 2029 in every scenario; 1 GW by 2031 is Low (base case). AI math adds confidence and a few percent; solar arrays and chip temperatures matter more.
patch.reader_hook: A gigawatt of orbital compute is about 4,000 Starmind-class satellites, 16,000-18,000 t and 110-180 Starship flights. AI-optimized radiator design might save about 350-1,400 t, or 4-14 flights (an assumption). Qualifying chips and memory to run about 30 C hotter would save more (about 1,900 t per GW in 33FG's model), and solar arrays, over half the satellite's mass, matter most.

patch.thesis: If AI plans and checks robot work, lunar and Mars robots do severalfold more work per operator by about 2029 (base case, Medium). A self-running Moon base waits on heavy cargo landings (Low by 2031); oxygen plants wait on anode life, night survival and funding.
patch.reader_hook: A 2024 molten-regolith electrolysis rig made 0.07 kg of oxygen an hour and NASA's MOXIE made 12 g/h on Mars, against about 1.1 kg/h for a 10 t/yr lunar plant and about 65 kg/h for a Starship return. And the unknown form of polar ice swings excavation cost by two to three orders of magnitude.

patch.thesis: If AI does the theory and inference behind missions, science per dollar rises from archives and satellite methane data get honest error bars by 2028 (Medium, base case). Launch dates hold: LISA still flies in 2035, and the Habitable Worlds Observatory moves at budget pace.
patch.reader_hook: The waveform physics LISA needs to hear small bodies spiral into giant black holes (second-order self-force) exists today only for circular orbits around non-spinning black holes. The base case finishes it around 2030, roughly three to five years ahead of the pre-AI path (analyst judgment). LISA still launches in 2035.

patch.thesis: If AI makes orbit, collision and space-weather forecasts honest, AI-designed trajectories fly and million-object screening exists by 2029, though SpaceX's Stargaze tracking narrows AI's share. Safe low orbit at 100,000 satellites is held back through 2031 by untracked 1-10 cm debris, regulators and uncooperative operators.
patch.reader_hook: Starlink already flies about 355,000 avoidance maneuvers a year at a collision threshold of 3 in 10 million, about 300 times stricter than the 1-in-10,000 norm. Meanwhile about 1.2 million 1-10 cm fragments go untracked, and solar-storm arrival forecasts have missed by about 13 hours on average for 11 years (about 10 hours for the best ensemble method).

patch.thesis: If AI and new diagnostics solve Hall-thruster electron transport, thrusters can be designed before they are built around 2030 (base case Low). Wear tests cap life credit at Low, a politically paced U.S. space reactor by 2031 is Low, and fusion propulsion waits past 2031.
patch.reader_hook: A 23,000-hour thruster life requirement means 2.6 years of continuous firing that no proof shortens. NASA already credits the 50% life margin by analysis; the open question is whether analysis can replace part of the test itself. Deuterium-helium-3 fusion has never burned at meaningful power, and a megawatt-class demonstrator needs only grams of helium-3, so fuel is not the gate.
